column4: Mostly yes. The notebook runs top to bottom and I was able to trace every figure in the report back to a cell that saves it, so as far as I could tell it should be straightforward to regenerate. One thing: environment.yaml says name: 215a while run.sh activates stat215a
column5: I didn't see any docstrings anywhere in the notebook, so anyone reading it has to guess what each block is doing. The map-drawing code also looks like it was copied out several times with the same setup each round, which would be worth pulling into one function. And one of the cells that merges on the state column doesn't appear to work — there's an empty plot warning sitting in the output.
column6: No typos or grammar problems that I could find, the writing is clean throughout. One thing I'd flag isn't grammar though: I didn't see the two Nerbonne & Kretzschmar papers cited anywhere in the body, only listed at the end, and reading them was the first thing the instructions asked for. I'd also cut the repeated paragraph about missing data, which is explained in section 2.1 and then said again in section 3.
column7: Yes, I think it reads as one piece — section 5 tying the stability results back to the silhouette caveat was the part I liked most. The one place it felt weaker was the jump from the Q68/Q69 analysis to the feature encoding, since I couldn't find anywhere that explains why the two- and four-question work got dropped from the main analysis.
column8: Described well, and I think the argument for restricting to the 40,061 people who answered everything is genuinely good, since finding that PC3 correlates 0.54 with how many questions people answered is real evidence rather than an assertion. What I didn't see is any look at the 7,410 people who got dropped, and if partial responders are concentrated in certain regions then every map later in the report is drawn from a biased sample.
column9: Q68 and Q69 is a good pairing and the reasoning makes sense to me. My issue is with the headline 55.8%, since it's counting whether the two answers are the same word but the questions don't offer the same choices (mimi shows up on Q68, gramma on Q69), so some people can never match. Your notebook flags this, which makes me think the report should keep that caveat (the 72.4% number is the more informative one anyway)
column10: The two maps looking almost identical is the best part for me, since it's the visual version of the high correlations you then put numbers on. I also liked that the legend sits outside the map instead of covering part of the country.
column11: The dots overlap enough that I think the figure mostly shows where people live rather than what they said, and since most people are in the big cities, the Northeast looks like the most interesting region just because it's the most crowded. Plotting the percentage using each term per state would match what you're actually claiming
column12: I agree with this, and the reason given for not scaling seems right to me, if you scaled everything, a word only 1% of people say would count as much as one 60% of people say. The PC3 finding about missing data is the strongest bit of analysis in the report. I'd only add that you try one scaling rather than both, so it's more of a demonstration than an assertion.
column13: Showing the scatter plot next to maps of PC1 and PC2 in order worked well for me. The scatter on its own is just a blob, which is the point that there aren't clean groups, and then the maps show those same two axes still have geography in them
column14: The elbow, silhouette, and eigengap plots are computed but I didn't see any of them saved into the report folder, so a reader has to take k=3 on faith without seeing the evidence. The silhouette one also looks like it's calculated on a sample of 5,000 rather than everyone, which the report doesn't mention.
column15: The two methods seem like a reasonable pairing, and I liked that you said outright that k=3 for spectral clustering was just to make it comparable rather than something the data pointed at. One thing to be careful of is that the two didn't see the same thing - k-means used all 40,061 people and all 468 features, spectral used 10,000 and the first 10 PCs — so when they disagree it might be the method, or it might just be the difference in inputs.
column16: The k-means map is the most interesting figure for me, because it shows three groups with a silhouette of only 0.032 still lining up with recognizable parts of the country. That's a nice result and the map makes it obvious.
column17: The color scale seems misleading to me. It runs continuously from 0 to 2 like a regular measurement, but cluster numbers aren't a scale - cluster 0 isn't "less than" cluster 1 — and the purple-to-yellow progression makes it look like there's a gradient when these are really just three labels sitting next to each other. Separate colors with a normal legend would read better.
column18: It's good that two checks were run, but I don't think the scores above 0.98 tell you much, since that mostly shows k-means finds the same answer from different starting points, which it tends to do anyway. The more useful check seems like it would be on the choices that actually shaped the data, for instance whether dropping 15.6% of respondents changes the picture
